title: Sound as sampled information
goals: Interpret an ordered sequence of sound-signal samples with a stated time interval
Explain why summaries or sparse samples can omit changes
Separate an audio recording, a transcript and an interpretation of meaning

prerequisite.prompt: Two image grids have the same number of black pixels. Why can their pictures differ?
prerequisite.answer: The total does not preserve positions. Different arrangements can contain the same number of black pixels.

vocabulary: A changing physical or recorded quantity that can carry information
A recorded value of a signal at a particular time in this lesson
The time between successive recorded samples
A representation of how a signal value changes over time
A text representation of spoken words, which may contain errors or omit sound details

blocks.text: Sound involves changing pressure in a medium such as air. A microphone responds to that variation and produces a changing signal. A digital recording stores measurements of the signal at successive times. The values are ordered: swapping their times changes the represented pattern.

We will use tiny invented sequences to study this idea on paper. Their values are arbitrary signal units, not decibels or a test of safe listening levels. Real audio uses many more samples, so our five-point examples should not be played as if they were a realistic recording of speech.

A recording must include enough information to interpret the values, including their time spacing and encoding. The sequence 0,2,0,2,0 does not by itself say how quickly the changes happened. This is similar to needing image dimensions as well as pixel values.

blocks.title: Three stages in a speech system
rows: Measure the changing signal at successive times
A transcript that may contain errors
A separate rule or model processes the text
blocks.caption: Recording, transcribing and interpreting are separate operations. A later stage can correctly process an incorrectly transcribed number.

blocks.text: There are five samples with four gaps between the first and last. Each gap is 1 millisecond, so the elapsed time from first to last is 4 milliseconds. If the same five values were spaced 2 milliseconds apart, they would span 8 milliseconds. Equal value lists with different timing do not describe the same time pattern.

The largest value in 0,2,0,2,0 is 2. The largest value in 0,0,2,0,0 is also 2. The first sequence reaches 2 twice at different times, while the second does so once. Keeping only the maximum loses that distinction, just as counting black pixels lost their arrangement.

Sparse measurements can also miss changes. If we inspect the first sequence only at times 0, 2 and 4 milliseconds, all retained values are 0. The two intervening values of 2 disappear from the record. It would be incorrect to conclude from these retained samples alone that the signal stayed at zero between them.

More frequent sampling can preserve faster changes under suitable recording conditions, but sampling frequency alone does not make every recording clear. Microphone placement, background sound, clipping and the recording format can also matter. We are studying one source of missing information, not a complete audio engineering specification.

A five-sample record has values 0,3,0,1,0 at times 0,2,4,6,8 milliseconds. Read the timing before answering. The first-to-last duration is the final time minus the initial time, not the sample count multiplied by the gap.

blocks.label: State the interval and first-to-last duration. If only times 0,4,8 are kept, list the retained values and identify a change the shorter record misses

blocks.text: To test a claim about the spaces between samples, construct another possible sequence that agrees at retained times but differs between them. If both match the stored record, that record alone cannot decide which intervening pattern occurred.

A transcript might record the words Fine, thank you while omitting a pause, a laugh or overlapping speech. It might also record the wrong words. Text can be useful for searching spoken content, but it is not the same representation as the audio. Do not infer a speaker's emotions with certainty from a short transcript.

In a voice calculator, audio saying sixteen can be transcribed as sixty. A calculator can then correctly divide sixty by four and return fifteen. Inspecting the intermediate transcript identifies the first mismatch. Confirming the interpreted numbers before acting can prevent this particular error from travelling into a later stage.

blocks.label: Explain one detail a transcript can preserve and one sound detail it may omit. Explain why a correct calculation does not prove the transcript was correct

workbook.title: Read samples and gaps
workbook.prompt: Five samples have values 0,3,0,1,0 at times 0,2,4,6,8 milliseconds. State the sample count, interval and elapsed time from first to last. Explain why there are four gaps.
workbook.answer: Five samples, a 2 ms interval, and 8 ms from first to last. Consecutive pairs make gaps 0-2, 2-4, 4-6 and 6-8: four gaps between five samples.

workbook.title: Inspect what was discarded
workbook.prompt: Retain only times 0,4,8 from W1. Write the retained values. Give one claim about the original signal that these retained values do not justify.
workbook.answer: The retained values are 0,0,0. They do not justify saying the signal was always zero or had no changes between those times; the original had values 3 and 1 at omitted times.

workbook.title: Compare equal summaries
workbook.prompt: Sequences A=0,2,0,2,0 and B=0,0,2,0,0 use the same time interval. State their maximum values and one difference the maximum discards. Name information that would preserve that difference.
workbook.answer: Both maxima are 2. A reaches 2 at two sample positions while B does so at one; their timing patterns differ. The full ordered samples with timing preserve the distinction. A maximum alone does not.

workbook.title: Construct a new hidden change
workbook.prompt: A record keeps values 0 at times 0,3,6 milliseconds. Construct two seven-sample sequences for every whole-millisecond time from 0 through 6 that agree with those retained values but differ at omitted times. Explain why the retained record cannot prove that nothing changed between measurements.
workbook.answer: One pair is [0,0,0,0,0,0,0] and [0,2,1,0,3,1,0]. Both have zero at indices/times 0,3,6, but the second changes at omitted times. The retained record is compatible with both, so it cannot establish an unchanged intervening signal. Any valid seven-value pair with those constraints is acceptable.

workbook.title: Check a speech pipeline
workbook.prompt: A recording says Set the timer for fourteen minutes. A transcript says forty minutes and the timer is set to 40. Name the first mismatch, propose a confirmation step and explain why the transcript cannot be treated as a complete copy of the recording.
workbook.answer: The first stated mismatch is fourteen becoming forty in transcription. Show or read back the interpreted duration and require correction/confirmation before starting the timer. A transcript may misstate words and omit tone, pauses and background sounds; correct handling of 40 does not validate the earlier transcription.

teacher.background: Keep the distinction between physical pressure variation, microphone signal and stored numerical samples. The examples use arbitrary nonnegative signal values to avoid introducing signed waveforms before they are needed; they do not model real speech faithfully. The lesson establishes ordering, time metadata and information loss. It does not teach a sampling theorem or make hearing-health claims.
materials: A time strip marked 0 through 8 milliseconds and paper sample-value cards
A cover sheet to hide omitted time positions
Printed fictional speech requests; recording students or opening accounts is unnecessary
sessions: Retrieve equal pixel counts with different arrangements. Replace position in space with position in time.
Trace the recording/transcript/processing diagram. Explain the invented units and times.
Count gaps physically between five sample cards. Compare the same values at two time intervals.
Complete W1 and W2, covering omitted positions and naming lost changes.
Compare the equal-maximum sequences. Require a specific difference, not only less information.
Complete W3 and practise constructing two records that agree at retained times.
Collect W4 independently, checking all seven positions and the three retained constraints.
Discuss W5 and the exit question. Close the unit by connecting evidence, representation, measurement, fitting, pixels and samples.
teacher.guidedAnswer: The interval is 2 ms and first-to-last duration 8 ms. Keeping 0,4,8 ms retains 0,0,0 and misses the 3 and 1 at 2 and 6 ms. A transcript can preserve estimated words but may omit pauses or background sounds. Correct arithmetic on a transcribed number does not establish that the number matches the recording.
misconceptions: Place five cards in a row and point to each space between them. The span ends at the last sample.
Equal recorded zeros prove the signal stayed zero
Reveal hidden sample cards between retained zeros. Construct both changing and unchanging originals.
A transcript is the recording in another file type
Compare the information each representation retains. Text estimates words and need not preserve sound details or exact wording.
teacher.assessment: W4 is secure when each proposed sequence has seven values, both satisfy the zero constraints at 0,3,6, at least one omitted position differs and the explanation identifies ambiguity between measurements. If positions are confused, reteach with labelled time boxes, then assess a fresh retained-time pattern.
teacher.support: Use large labelled boxes and tactile counters. Read values aloud while pointing to their time labels. No hearing-based task is required. Extension: ask whether doubling the interval changes the number of samples, the first-to-last duration or the stored values when the same list is replayed under the new timing convention.
teacher.next: Week 7 builds on this unit by defining categories operationally so different people can label the same evidence consistently.
